To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

pre-service teachers’ life history narratives reveal the complex ways in which they construct difference between themselves, as prospective teachers of English language learners (ELs), and others; they express a sense that their experiences in the classroom have prepared them to teach ELs, but their narratives suggest that their experiences are not sufficient; and they construct citizenship as a dimension that is related to their experiences as learners, but not necessarily to their experiences as teachers.

pre-service teachers’ constructions of difference are often based on a narrow and essentialist understanding of culture and that their sense of citizenship as teachers is often limited to a focus on their individual rights and responsibilities.

pre-service teachers’ constructions of difference and their imagined conceptions of citizenship as a dimension thereof, were shaped by their own life experiences, and their views of themselves as teachers of ELs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how pre-service teachers interpret and construct their identities and citizenship as prospective teachers of linguistically and culturally different learners.

how pre-service teachers construct and negotiate the boundaries of difference and community, how they interpret and express citizenship as a dimension in their life history narratives, and how their constructions of difference are related to their constructions of community.

the ways in which pre-service teachers construct and interpret citizenship as a dimension in the narratives of their own lives, and the ways in their interpretations of their own lives influence their imagined (or constructed) conceptions of ELs and ELs as participants in classroom communities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study has shown that the pre-service teachers’ stories about themselves and their experiences in school are not simply stories of individual lives.
the narratives of the participants in this study were constructed around the theme of “difference” and the subthemes of “belonging,” “community,” “citizenship,” and “diversity.”
this study shows the importance of citizenship as an element of diversity and how it is related to difference.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

pre-service teachers’ constructions of citizenship and belonging in their own narratives are often in tension with the dominant ideologies of citizenship and belonging that they encounter and that they are often unaware of the ways that their constructions reflect dominant ideologies.

the findings of our research suggest that the pre-service teachers in our sample were not able to construct a sense of community membership or citizenship that would be inclusive of the ELs in their future classrooms.
pre-service teachers’ life history narratives reveal the ways in which difference and citizenship are constructed and interpreted through their personal experiences and their perceptions of others.
The main takeaway from our work is that
pre-service teachers’ understandings of citizenship are influenced by their experiences with difference.
teacher educators need to be aware of how pre-service teachers are socialized into dominant ideologies and how their own narratives are shaped by these ideologies.
the ways in which pre-service teachers construct themselves and others as members of a community of learners and participants in school and society are important to consider in teacher education.
